author: Ibn Battuta
title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta, A.D. 1325 to 1354, vols. 1 to 4
publisher: Hakluyt Society (Cambridge University Press for vols. 1 to 3; Hakluyt Society, London, for vol. 4)
translator: H. A. R. Gibb (vols. 1 to 3); vol. 4 translation by Gibb, completed with notes by C. F. Beckingham
note: Egypt in 1326 is vol. 1, pp. 18 to 71; Mali in 1352 to 1353 is vol. 4, pp. 946 on. His account of Egypt is compiled from several visits. Use only what he says he saw.

author: Nehemia Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, eds.
title: Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History
note: 492 pp. Al-Umari on Mansa Musa in Cairo, pp. 269 to 273. The twelve years of cheap gold is al-Umari's claim alone; Schultz 2006 doubts it.

author: S. D. Goitein
title: Letters of Medieval Jewish Traders
note: xviii + 359 pp. Geniza letters; shows how merchants and agents worked, not events of the 1330s.

author: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti
title: La pratica della mercatura, ed. Allan Evans
note: liv + 443 pp. Edition of the Italian, no translation. A merchant's handbook; its lists guide, they do not record prices.

author: Robert S. Lopez and Irving W. Raymond
title: Medieval Trade in the Mediterranean World: Illustrative Documents
translator: Robert S. Lopez and Irving W. Raymond
note: xi + 458 pp. Records of Civilization, no. 52. Contracts, letters and manuals in translation.

author: Ibn Khaldun
title: The Muqaddimah: An Introduction to History
publisher: Pantheon Books (2nd ed. Princeton University Press, 1967)
note: His account of the plague of 1348 is in vol. 1, about p. 64. He writes decades after the plague and gives his own views on trade.

author: Ibn Jubayr
title: The Travels of Ibn Jubayr
note: 430 pp. Describes the Qus to Aydhab route 140 years before the game. Use for how the route worked, not for 1324 prices.

author: S. D. Goitein
title: A Mediterranean Society, vol. 1: Economic Foundations
note: xxvi + 550 pp. Geniza merchants' letters and contracts. Its picture of one free Mediterranean society has been qualified.

author: Abraham L. Udovitch
title: Partnership and Profit in Medieval Islam
period: legal texts of the 8th to 11th century
note: xii + 282 pp. The qirad and other partnerships from jurists' handbooks; shows the rules, not how often they were kept.

author: Janet L. Abu-Lughod
title: Before European Hegemony: The World System A.D. 1250 to 1350
note: 443 pp. Cairo is ch. 9. Use for the map of links, not for the cause of anything; her account of Egypt and of decline is criticised.

author: Eliyahu Ashtor
title: A Social and Economic History of the Near East in the Middle Ages
note: 384 pp. Also issued by the University of California Press. Rests on a Mamluk decline thesis that later historians dispute.

author: Eliyahu Ashtor
title: Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages
note: xxii + 599 pp. Price series from Venetian and Genoese records are the useful part; the decline thesis is disputed.

author: Frederic C. Lane
title: Venice: A Maritime Republic
note: xiii + 505 pp. Galley convoys; the papal bans on trade with Egypt and their licences.

author: David Abulafia
title: The Great Sea: A Human History of the Mediterranean
note: 783 pp. A general history for the teacher's frame, not a source for a card.

author: K. N. Chaudhuri
title: Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean: An Economic History from the Rise of Islam to 1750
note: xiv + 269 pp. Monsoon timing and the Red Sea trade.

author: George F. Hourani
title: Arab Seafaring in the Indian Ocean in Ancient and Early Medieval Times
note: viii + 131 pp.; expanded edition by John Carswell, 1995, xvii + 189 pp. Sound on the basics of dhows and monsoons, old on the rest.

author: Robert Irwin
title: The Middle East in the Middle Ages: The Early Mamluk Sultanate, 1250 to 1382
note: 180 pp. The sultan al-Nasir Muhammad's reigns and the emirs.

author: Andre Raymond
title: Cairo
period: Cairo from its founding; Mamluk chapters
note: viii + 436 pp. Markets, wakalas, the size of the city. Translator named from MER-10; not seen in a catalogue record. Population figures are disputed.

author: Boaz Shoshan
title: Popular Culture in Medieval Cairo
note: xv + 148 pp. Festivals and everyday life.

author: Ira M. Lapidus
title: Muslim Cities in the Later Middle Ages
note: xiv + 307 pp. Old; some claims about Cairo were revised later.

author: Michael W. Dols
title: The Black Death in the Middle East
note: 408 pp. Alexandria in autumn 1347; Cairo struck in autumn 1348 as the secondary reports have it (pages unchecked). Death tolls are the chroniclers' and Dols says so.

author: Michael W. Dols
title: The Second Plague Pandemic and Its Recurrences in the Middle East: 1347 to 1894
publisher: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 22, no. 2, pp. 162 to 189 (Brill)
note: Later waves of plague.

author: Stuart J. Borsch
title: The Black Death in Egypt and England: A Comparative Study
note: xii + 195 pp. Argues Egypt's damage was larger and longer than England's because of how land was held; a note resting on this work alone says so.

author: Nehemia Levtzion
title: Ancient Ghana and Mali
note: x + 283 pp. Dates and the reach of Mali rest on few sources.

author: Timothy F. Garrard
title: Myth and Metrology: The Early Trans-Saharan Gold Trade
publisher: Journal of African History 23, no. 4, pp. 443 to 461 (Cambridge University Press)
note: How much gold moved and in what units; contested.

author: Peter Jackson
title: The Mongols and the Islamic World: From Conquest to Conversion
note: xxi + 614 pp. The Ilkhanate under Abu Said, who died at the end of 1335 without an heir; contested only on why it broke up.

author: Bernard Lewis
title: Race and Slavery in the Middle East: An Historical Enquiry
note: vii + 184 pp. For the About page only: that the trade ran on these routes is not disputed; Lewis's framing is.

author: Warren C. Schultz
title: Mansa Musa's Gold in Mamluk Cairo: A Reappraisal of a World Civilizations Anecdote
publisher: Harrassowitz (in History and Historiography of Post-Mongol Central Asia and the Middle East, eds. Pfeiffer and Quinn)
note: Not one of the 27; added by MER-20 and not yet read in full. Cairo's gold rate fell about 25:1 to 20:1 from 1324 and is one of several short swings; al-Umari alone says twelve years. Check pages on a library copy before a card cites it.

author: David Peacock and Andrew Peacock
title: The Enigma of 'Aydhab: a Medieval Islamic Port on the Red Sea Coast
publisher: International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 37, no. 1, pp. 32 to 48
note: Read end to end. Qus as the Nile port for Red Sea goods and Quseir's shorter desert leg, p. 33; the north wind over the Red Sea, p. 33; the desert crossing, p. 34; Beja and Aydhab's revenues, pp. 35 and 38. The decline of Aydhab is an open question (p. 45); the 1426 destruction story is Leo Africanus's and Garcin (1972) rejects it.

author: David Jacoby
title: Between Venice and Alexandria: Trade and the Movement of Precious Metals in the Early Mamluk Period
note: Read at pp. 116 to 137. The embargo of 1291, p. 116; Venice's galley convoys of 1301 to 1312, p. 117; money and the Alexandria mint, pp. 121 to 123; Famagusta as port of call, p. 133; the ban of 1323, the envoy of August 1344 and the treaty of 1345, pp. 135 to 137.

author: T. M. P. Duggan
title: From Mid-October to the End of March: Voyaging in the Medieval Mediterranean
note: Read in full. Winter bans on sailing were a legal fiction, not a closed sea (p. 277); his list of winter voyages includes Alexandria to Crete in December 1319 (p. 294). His p. 294 puts the plague at Alexandria in spring 1347, which disagrees with the autumn other notes use.

author: Avner Greif
title: Institutions and the Path to the Modern Economy: Lessons from Medieval Trade, ch. 4
note: Chapter 4 read at the Genoa and Tabriz passage, which cites Lopez 1943, pp. 183 to 184: Tabriz's ruler seized the goods of many Genoese in 1340 and Genoa embargoed Tabriz; the 1344 reopening ended in robbery and killings.

author: Robert S. Lopez
title: (title not recorded in the notes; cited by Greif 2006 as Lopez 1943, pp. 183 to 184, on Genoa and Tabriz)
note: Not read. Held here so a claim can cite it as Greif does; look up the title and journal before the About page names it.

author: Eric Vallet
title: Le marche des epices d'Alexandrie et les mutations du grand commerce de la mer Rouge (XIVe-XVe siecle)
publisher: Alexandrie medievale 4 (Etudes alexandrines 24, Cairo), pp. 213 to 228
note: Read in an author's deposit. Al-Maqrizi on pepper in April 1347, 46 dirhams a ratl and then 5 at the pilgrims' arrival, p. 216; Ashtor on a mid-century pepper price, pp. 213 to 214. His reading that the Aydhab road failed is his inference.

author: Tsugitaka Sato
title: Sugar in the Economic Life of Mamluk Egypt
publisher: Mamluk Studies Review 8, no. 2, pp. 87 to 107
note: Read, page numbers printed. Sugar growing in Upper Egypt, pp. 91 to 99; the load (himl) and the Alexandria canal, p. 98; units and epidemic prices, p. 103; the Ramadan grant of 1,000 and later 3,000 qintars, pp. 104 to 105.

author: Tsugitaka Sato
title: Slave Traders and Karimi Merchants during the Mamluk Period: A Comparative Study
publisher: Mamluk Studies Review 10, no. 1, pp. 141 to 156
note: Karimi families including Ibn Kuwayk, p. 147; their goods and the office of spice, p. 149; a loose confederation, p. 150. Cited here for the Karimi pages only.

author: Benjamin Arbel
title: The Last Decades of Venice's Trade with the Mamluks
publisher: Mamluk Studies Review 8, no. 2, pp. 37 to 86
period: about 1480 to 1517, with notes on the 14th century
note: Read to note 42. The Alexandria qintar jarwi of 95.4 kg, p. 47 n. 42; copper imported from northern Anatolia in the 14th and early 15th century, about p. 50 (page not confirmed). Its cargo lists are of the late 15th century.

author: Stuart J. Borsch
title: Plague Depopulation and Irrigation Decay in Medieval Egypt
publisher: The Medieval Globe 1, no. 1, pp. 125 to 156
note: Read. Al-Maqrizi's ship at Alexandria in 1347 and Cairo's peak in December 1348, p. 125; he calls al-Maqrizi a muhtasib as well as a historian, p. 125; the Nile flood and its monsoon rains. Borsch's larger argument about land holding is disputed.

author: Claudia Maria Tresso
title: Ibn Battuta's 'Prayer of Damascus': A window on to Damascus in the hell of the Black Death (Part Two)
note: Read. Cairo's gatherings and height in November and December 1348, p. 220; Alexandria's peak, p. 208 n. 3; al-Maqrizi's dates, p. 217 n. 46.

author: Michael W. Dols
title: Ibn al-Wardi's Risalat al-naba' 'an al-waba': a translation of a major source for the history of the Black Death in the Middle East
publisher: pp. 443 to 455 (the volume that holds it is not recorded in the notes)
note: Not read; its page range comes from Tresso's bibliography. Held so a card on the merchants' news from the Crimea can cite it; the Rajab 747 report is unchecked.

author: Michael W. Dols
title: The Comparative Communal Responses to the Black Death in Muslim and Christian Societies
note: The court at Siryaqus from 1 Rajab 749 (25 September 1348) to the end of Ramadan, notes 31 and 32; the printed page of the passage was not visible. It does not say the plague began in Cairo on that day.

author: Hadrien Collet
title: Le pelerinage total de Mansa Moussa (14e siecle), in Les pelerinages en Islam
note: Departure 16 Shawwal 724 (14 October 1324); Hajj 4 to 9 December; a stay of a little over three months. Read through an extract. Collet's 2019 article in History in Africa 46 was not reached.

author: Frederic Bauden
title: The Sons of al-Nasir Muhammad and the Politics of Puppets: Where Did It All Start?
publisher: Mamluk Studies Review 13, no. 1, pp. 53 to 81
note: Read in full. Eight sons, two grandsons and two great-grandsons of al-Nasir Muhammad ruled to 1382, p. 53; Abu Bakr's death, p. 63; Anuk's wedding, p. 65; the sultan's pilgrimage, p. 66; the death and the succession, pp. 74 and 76. 'Puppets' is disputed by other historians.

author: Abdullah Mesut Agir
title: Al-Makrizi's Khitat and the Markets in Cairo during the Mamluks Era
period: al-Maqrizi, early 15th century, describing earlier markets
note: Read through character 100,000 of 123,450; the copy had no page numbers, so a claim cites a section or a footnote. The muhtasib's finding of 1341, section 1 n. 95; qaysariyya, funduq, khan and wikala as one type of building, Background n. 17.

author: Johan Soderberg
title: Grain Prices in Cairo and Europe in the Middle Ages
publisher: Research in Economic History 24, pp. 189 to 216
note: Read. The 1336 import of grain from Syria and Palestine, p. 198 (note 7); Sabra's list of ten shortages, note 8.

author: James A. N. Hill
title: The Papacy and the Eastern Mediterranean 1305 to 1362
note: Read the passages on trade licences, pp. 49 to 50 and 57 to 60. An unpublished thesis; cite it only for what it reports from the 1345 treaty and the licence registers. No sign the Genoese or Catalans stopped trading with Egypt, p. 49.

author: Adam Sabra
title: Poverty and Charity in Medieval Islam: Mamluk Egypt, 1250 to 1517
note: 192 pp. Chapter 6, food shortages and famines, begins p. 134; the case studies run pp. 138 to 164 (page range from Soderberg's note 8). The book was not reached; contents and introduction only.

author: (author of each entry not read; look up before use)
title: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, entries Muhammed b. Kalavun, es-Salih Ebu'l-Fida, el-Kamil Sa'ban, Hasan b. Muhammed b. Kalavun, Memlukler
note: Hijri and Julian day dates for the sultans' accessions and deaths, 1341 to 1347; each matches the tabular calendar. The year of each entry and its page were not recorded and must be added from the printed volume (the year here is a placeholder, not a date).

author: Ibn Battuta
title: Travels in Asia and Africa 1325 to 1354
note: Gibb's abridged selection, read as teaching-site excerpts (Egypt, the Sahara and Mali, China), so most passages have no page number; the China and porcelain passage is pp. 282 to 283 and the Taghaza and Mali pages are about pp. 317 to 335. Prices of salt at Walata and Mali are of 1352 to 1353.

author: S. D. Goitein
title: Commercial and Family Partnerships in the Countries of Medieval Islam
note: Written from Geniza contracts, not from law books. The worker's smaller share, normally one third, and no share in the loss, p. 317; a manager who broke the contract's terms paid the whole loss, p. 327. About 1000 to 1250, so it shows how partnerships worked, not events of the 1330s.

author: Niall Christie
title: Reconstructing Life in Medieval Alexandria from an Eighth/Fourteenth Century Waqf Document
publisher: Mamluk Studies Review 8, no. 2, pp. 165 to about 185
note: The sultan's property in Alexandria sold or listed on 16 April 1326: a glass-works that was first a soap-works, a silk funduq, sugar cane.

author: Bethany J. Walker
title: Rethinking Mamluk Textiles
note: Read. Silk and linen in Alexandria and Cairo, pp. 168 to 172; European woollens as a 15th-century mass import, about p. 171, quoting Ashtor.

author: Walter J. Fischel
title: The Spice Trade in Mamluk Egypt
publisher: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 1, no. 2, pp. 157 to 174
period: Mamluk period, with the main evidence from the 15th century
note: The Karimi and the office that watched their spice imports, pp. 167 to 168; Fischel says the prices and profits of the spice trade are not sufficiently documented, p. 168. Ashtor disagrees with Fischel on how tightly the Karimi were organised.

author: Amalia Levanoni
title: The Mamluks in Egypt and Syria: The Turkish Mamluk Sultanate (648 to 784/1250 to 1382) and the Circassian Mamluk Sultanate (784 to 923/1382 to 1517), in The New Cambridge History of Islam, vol. 2
note: Read as the chapter summary only. Muslim rulers bought Turkish soldiers from Central Asia and the Eurasian steppes to serve in the army that became the Mamluk state. The volume editor is Maribel Fierro.

author: Carl F. Petry
title: Ethos of the 'Slave-Soldiers' Regime, ch. 2 of The Mamluk Sultanate: A History
note: Read as the abstract only. Cadets were brought in first from the Qipjaq steppe and later from Circassia; the abstract gives no date for the change, so no text here may.

author: Janel Fontaine
title: Review of Hannah Barker, That Most Precious Merchandise: The Mediterranean Trade in Black Sea Slaves, 1260 to 1500 (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2019)
note: A review read in full on the page; Barker's book was not reached. Names Caffa as a Genoese colony and Tana as a Mongol port, and says writers of crusade plans repeatedly called for an embargo on this trade with Egypt. The reviewer's name is printed on the review page.

author: Jeffrey Miner
title: Review of Hannah Barker, That Most Precious Merchandise (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2019)
note: A review read in full on the page. Thousands of people a year were shipped from the northern Black Sea shore to Egypt and Italy, and Alexandria had special markets and brokers for the trade (p. 96 for brokers); the review does not date the figure to the 1320s to 1340s.

author: Emily Sohmer Tai
title: Review of Hannah Barker, That Most Precious Merchandise (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2019)
publisher: Center for Cultural and World History, review of 6 January 2023
note: A review read in full on the page. Used only for Tana: under the Mongol khanate of the Golden Horde but managed by Venice.

author: Lorenzo Pubblici
title: Some Remarks on the Slave Trade in the Heart of the Golden Horde (14th Century) in the Wake of C. Verlinden's Research
publisher: Golden Horde Review 5, no. 3, pp. 566 to 576
note: Read as text. Tana at the mouth of the Don, a trading outpost for Venetians and Genoese, p. 566.

author: Craig Perry
title: Historicizing Slavery in the Medieval Islamic World
publisher: International Journal of Middle East Studies 49, no. 1, pp. 133 to 138
note: Read as the partial text on the publisher's page. Nubia was a major source of enslaved people for Egypt, moved north by river and overland, but the old treaty called the baqt was not responsible for most of them.
